name: Ashwagandha
lead: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera), also called Indian ginseng or winter cherry, is a shrub of the nightshade family whose root has been used for centuries in Ayurveda, the traditional medicine of India [1][25]. In looksmaxxing and fitness circles it is taken as a supplement, as root powder or standardized extract, to support the things that shape a physique and a rested, healthy appearance: training recovery, strength and muscle gain, stress and sleep, and hormone health [1][14][15][100].

The link to looks runs through several chains. Lower stress and better sleep are associated with better recovery and training consistency, and proponents also hope for higher testosterone and lean-mass gains from training with it [8][5][3]. Its main constituents are withanolides, steroid-like lactones such as withaferin A, which resemble compounds in Asian ginseng and give the plant its nickname [1].

Research includes meta-analyses of randomized trials reporting lower stress and anxiety scores and a small improvement in sleep [3][4][5], and a handful of small trials in people doing resistance training that measured strength, muscle size, testosterone and endurance [8][9][10]. Reviewers and health agencies describe the trials as mostly small and using different preparations, and note rare reports of liver injury [1][100].

paras: In strength-training communities ashwagandha is grouped with recovery and hormone-support supplements. T Nation members mention it in training logs, deployment supply lists and TRT recovery logs, often next to tongkat ali, fadogia and magnesium [14][15][16][17][37]. A forum post describes a social-media video promoting it as a testosterone booster [18].

Users describe three main goals. The first is stress and sleep, on the reasoning that sleep and lower stress hormones help recovery and body composition. The second is training performance, specifically strength and muscle gain. The third is testosterone support, either for general vitality or alongside hormone-therapy regimens [15][17][22]. The NCCIH notes that people take it for stress, anxiety, sleep, male infertility and athletic performance [100].

Ashwagandha root is a rasayana in Ayurveda, a class of tonics intended to promote vitality and longevity [25]. Reviews describe more than 3,000 years of use in Indian systems of medicine [7]. Research has examined stress, anxiety, sleep, thyroid function, cognition and sexual health [3][4][5][11][13][19][20].

W. somnifera is an evergreen shrub typically 35 to 75 cm tall with oval leaves, small bell-shaped flowers and orange-red fruit. It is native across the Middle East, Africa and the Indian subcontinent and is cultivated in the drier parts of India [1]. Linnaeus described the species in 1753 [1]. The common name combines Sanskrit words for horse and smell, referring to the root's odor, while the species name somnifera means sleep-inducing [1].

About 40 withanolides and 12 alkaloids have been isolated, along with other steroidal lactones and sitoindosides [1]. Withanolides are C28 steroidal lactones built on an ergostane framework [104]. Commercial products are sold as whole root powder or as extracts standardized to a withanolide percentage, and trials often use proprietary extracts such as KSM-66 [8][9][102][103].

Ashwagandha is usually marketed as an adaptogen, a term coined in 1947 by the Soviet toxicologist Nikolai Lazarev for substances thought to raise the body's non-specific resistance to stress [101]. Soviet researchers developed the idea further, and a 1969 review by Brekhman and Dardymov is a key source [101].

Critics and regulators treat the category differently. The European Medicines Agency's herbal committee stated in a 2008 reflection paper that the term is not accepted in mainstream pharmacology or clinical practice in the EU, and Wikipedia reports that the FDA issued warning letters in 2020 to 2023 to supplement makers whose adaptogen products carried unapproved health claims [101]. Proponents counter that adaptogens are defined by their observed effects on stress-response markers, such as cortisol, in trials [4][12].

A 2022 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials (1,002 participants) found that ashwagandha reduced anxiety and stress scores compared with placebo, with very high heterogeneity between trials [3]. A 2024 meta-analysis of nine trials (558 patients) reported significant effects on the Perceived Stress Scale, the Hamilton Anxiety Scale and serum cortisol, with mild to moderate adverse events in four trials [4].

A 2021 meta-analysis of five trials (400 participants) found a small but significant effect on sleep, more prominent in people with insomnia and in trials of at least eight weeks [5]. Individual randomized trials of standardized extracts in stressed adults, including a 60-day placebo-controlled study, reported lower stress and cortisol measures [11][12]. A qualitative analysis of a trial in college students recorded participants' perceptions of stress, sleep, energy and mental clarity [26]. Wikipedia states that current clinical evidence is not sufficient to confirm safety or efficacy [1].

The best-known exercise study is an 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 57 untrained men (50 completed) who followed a supervised resistance program with either KSM-66 root extract or starch capsules [8][102]. The ashwagandha group's bench-press maximum rose about 46 kg versus 26 kg, leg-extension strength and arm and chest size rose more, body-fat percentage fell about 3.5 versus 1.5 percent, and testosterone rose about 96 versus 18 ng/dL; thigh size did not differ significantly [102]. The authors noted the small sample, short duration and young untrained participants, and the paper's creatine-kinase recovery figures are internally inconsistent [102]. The extract was supplied by companies named in the acknowledgments [102].

A multicenter 8-week trial in 80 healthy adults who already trained (73 analysed) reported larger gains in bench-press and leg-press strength, chest and arm circumference and VO2max with the same extract than with placebo, and no reported adverse events; the supplier supplied the product and no grants supported the work [9][103].

A 2026 systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials (599 participants) found a pooled benefit of g = 0.47 for exercise performance, with the most consistent result in aerobic endurance (g = 0.54); the strength estimate (g = 0.48) was positive but not statistically significant, power and muscular endurance showed no clear change, and the prediction interval crossed zero [10]. The authors list small numbers of trials, differing products and risk-of-bias concerns as limitations [10].

A 2023 review of ashwagandha and the endocrine system concluded that it may affect endocrine function positively but described the literature as heterogeneous [6]. A randomized placebo-controlled trial in subclinical hypothyroid patients examined thyroid markers [13]. The NCCIH says limited evidence suggests that two to four months of use may raise testosterone and improve sperm quality, and that evidence is insufficient for athletic performance [100].

Registered trials include studies in footballers' exercise performance (NCT06264986), muscle-damage prevention (NCT06900569), adolescent football recovery (NCT07890935), sleep (NCT07151261), sexual health in men and women (NCT05840731, NCT05831241), college-student stress (NCT05430685), cognition after chemotherapy (NCT04092647) and a root-extract safety study (NCT06261476) [27][28][29][30][19][31][32][20][33].

Reviews describe withanolides as modulating the stress axis, lowering cortisol and affecting GABAergic and inflammatory signalling [6][7]. Narrative reviews also describe immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects, largely from preclinical work [7][24]. Much of the proposed mechanism for testosterone or muscle effects remains inferred, since exercise trials rarely measured relevant biomarkers [10].

Commonly reported side effects are diarrhea, headache, sedation, nausea and stomach upset [1][100]. Wikipedia and the NCCIH describe use up to about three months as generally well tolerated, with long-term safety not established [1][100].

Ashwagandha has been linked to herb-induced liver injury, rarely, and particularly in people with existing liver disease [1][100]. Both sources advise avoiding it in pregnancy, and the NCCIH adds breastfeeding, before surgery, and autoimmune or thyroid disorders; possible interactions listed include diabetes and blood-pressure medicines, immunosuppressants, sedatives, anticonvulsants and thyroid hormone [100]. People with hormone-sensitive prostate cancer are advised to avoid it because it may raise testosterone [1][100]. A pharmacological review discusses toxicity aspects [7].

In the United States ashwagandha is sold as a dietary supplement, which the FDA does not approve before sale; manufacturers are responsible for safety and labeling [100]. Its adaptogen marketing sits within the broader regulatory discussion of unapproved health claims [101].

On T Nation ashwagandha appears mainly in supplement lists, training logs and TRT threads. Some users report benefits for stress and sleep or testosterone; one reports not recommending it, another says it works best when taken in cycles because it seems to lose effect, and a third noted a testosterone rise after stopping an antioxidant product containing it while naming other possible explanations [21][22][23]. It is often combined with other herbs such as tongkat ali, fadogia and fenugreek [15][16].

Ashwagandha is commonly discussed alongside other herbal hormone-support supplements such as fenugreek and tongkat ali, sleep aids such as magnesium, and recovery nutrition for resistance training [15][16][37].

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums ashwagandha is discussed as a stress, sleep and testosterone-support supplement, usually inside multi-supplement stacks, with mixed personal experiences [14][21][22][17].

claims.believers: Social-media clips and forum users promote it as a testosterone booster; one user reports taking it with tongkat ali and fadogia [15][18].
claims.experts: A 2015 trial in untrained men reported a larger testosterone rise than placebo alongside resistance training, though post-trial group values did not differ significantly [102]; the NCCIH says limited evidence suggests a rise after two to four months [100].

claims.believers: Users take it for stress and for night-time wind-down [22][17].
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report reduced stress, anxiety and cortisol scores, with substantial heterogeneity [3][4].

claims.believers: Posters list it in bedtime stacks with magnesium [37].
claims.experts: A 2021 meta-analysis found a small but significant effect on sleep, larger in people with insomnia [5].

claims.believers: Lifters include it for training support and recovery [14][16].
claims.experts: Two 8-week trials of one branded extract reported larger strength and size gains than placebo [102][103]; a 2026 meta-analysis found a significant benefit for aerobic endurance and a non-significant strength estimate [10].

claims.believers: Users cite it as a recovery aid in training logs [14][16].
claims.experts: The 2015 trial reported lower creatine kinase with ashwagandha, though its authors' figures are internally inconsistent [102]; trials of recovery in footballers are registered [27][29].

claims.claim: It loses effectiveness and should be cycled
claims.believers: One TRT-log poster says it works best when cycled because it seems to lose effect [22].
claims.experts: No published study has examined tolerance or cycling of ashwagandha.

claims.claim: Ashwagandha is harmless because it is natural
claims.believers: Users include it routinely in daily stacks [16].
claims.experts: Rare cases of liver injury are documented, and avoidance in pregnancy is advised [1][100].

angle.text: People take ashwagandha to support the habits that build a better-looking body: sleeping well, managing stress and recovering between sessions. Small trials of resistance-trained adults have measured bench-press strength, arm and chest size and body fat alongside it [8][9].
